name: Southern Rock
blurb: Twin guitars, Georgia mud and the long jams that put the South on the radio.

questions.prompt: Which band's name came from a high school gym teacher who sent boys with long hair to the principal?
questions.fact: Leonard Skinner taught at Robert E. Lee High School in Jacksonville, Florida. The band bent the spelling and later made peace with him.

questions.prompt: Which musician died in a motorcycle accident in Macon, Georgia, in October 1971?
questions.fact: Bassist Berry Oakley died in a similar motorcycle crash a year later, a few blocks from the same spot.

questions.prompt: In "The Devil Went Down to Georgia", what prize does the Devil put up against Johnny's soul?
questions.fact: The Charlie Daniels Band's 1979 hit won a Grammy in 1980 for Best Country Vocal Performance by a duo or group.

questions.prompt: "Sweet Home Alabama" was Lynyrd Skynyrd's answer to songs by which singer?
questions.fact: Young's "Southern Man" and "Alabama" criticized the South, and Ronnie Van Zant answered with a song of his own. Van Zant said he was a fan of Young's music.

questions.prompt: Which band recorded the 1971 live album At Fillmore East?
questions.fact: It was recorded over two nights in March 1971 and is widely regarded as one of the finest live rock albums ever made.

questions.prompt: Billy Gibbons got his start in a Texas psychedelic band that opened for Jimi Hendrix. What was it called?
questions.fact: Hendrix is said to have given Gibbons a pink Stratocaster, and the band's regional hit "99th Floor" came before ZZ Top formed.

questions.prompt: Which Lynyrd Skynyrd song starts as a slow ballad and ends with a long guitar jam?
questions.fact: The album version runs more than nine minutes, and most of that is the fast guitar finale.

questions.prompt: Gregg Allman's signature keyboard sound came from which instrument?
questions.fact: Gregg wrote "Whipping Post" and "Midnight Rider", and his gritty voice anchored the band's sound.

questions.prompt: Which Rolling Stones song was cut at Muscle Shoals Sound in December 1969?
questions.fact: They also recorded "Wild Horses" there that week, only days before the Altamont concert.

questions.prompt: Which Lynyrd Skynyrd singer died in the plane crash of October 1977?
questions.fact: Van Zant, guitarist Steve Gaines and backup singer Cassie Gaines were among those killed. The album Street Survivors had come out days earlier.

questions.prompt: After the October 1977 plane crash, MCA changed the cover of which Lynyrd Skynyrd album because it showed the band in flames?
questions.fact: The album had come out only days before, and the flame cover was replaced with a plain black one, though later reissues restored the original image.

questions.prompt: Which rhythm section from Muscle Shoals is name-checked in "Sweet Home Alabama"?
questions.fact: The Swampers played on hits by Aretha Franklin, Wilson Pickett and Paul Simon, and had a studio of their own.

questions.prompt: Which producer, famous for the organ on "Like a Rolling Stone", signed Skynyrd and produced their early albums?
questions.fact: Kooper discovered the band playing at Funocchio's, a club in Atlanta, and signed them to his Sounds of the South label.

questions.prompt: 38 Special's Donnie Van Zant is the younger brother of which Skynyrd founder?
questions.fact: Another brother, Johnny Van Zant, took over as Skynyrd's singer when the band reformed in 1987.

questions.prompt: Which Allman Brothers guitarist wrote "Ramblin' Man"?
questions.fact: Betts has said he wrote a country-tinged song inspired by Hank Williams's "Ramblin' Man", an unusual move for a blues-rock band.

questions.prompt: Capricorn Records, home of the Allman Brothers, was founded by the former manager of which soul singer?
questions.fact: Phil Walden founded the label in Macon, Georgia, in 1969, and Macon was also Redding's hometown.

questions.prompt: The Allman Brothers Band had two drummers. One was Butch Trucks. Who was the other?
questions.fact: The twin-drum, twin-guitar format gave the band its rolling, jazz-tinged power.

questions.prompt: Which 1983 ZZ Top album includes "Gimme All Your Lovin'", "Sharp Dressed Man" and "Legs"?
questions.fact: The cover shows a customized 1933 Ford coupe, which appeared in the band's videos on MTV.

questions.prompt: Which Skynyrd keyboardist first came to the band as a roadie?
questions.fact: Powell impressed Ronnie Van Zant with his piano playing, and his keyboard part opens "Free Bird".

questions.prompt: Which Allman Brothers instrumental is now known as the theme to the BBC's Top Gear?
questions.fact: Dickey Betts named the tune for his young daughter, and wrote it on acoustic guitar before the band added the full arrangement.

questions.prompt: The Allman Brothers' version of "Statesboro Blues" was a cover of a song by which bluesman?
questions.fact: McTell recorded the song in 1928, and Duane Allman took the slide-guitar arrangement from Taj Mahal's version.

questions.prompt: ZZ Top's "La Grange" is about a notorious brothel near La Grange, Texas. What was it called?
questions.fact: Fans and critics have long noted the resemblance to Hooker's boogie groove.

choices: A blind piano tuner from their rehearsal building

questions.prompt: Skynyrd's "Call Me the Breeze" was written by which songwriter?
questions.fact: Cale also wrote "After Midnight" and "Cocaine", both made famous by Eric Clapton.

questions.prompt: The Atlanta Rhythm Section grew out of the lineup that recorded the hit "Spooky". What was that group called?

questions.prompt: Before his own hits, Charlie Daniels played sessions in Nashville for which songwriter?

questions.prompt: Which member of ZZ Top is the only one of the three without a long beard?

questions.prompt: The Allman Brothers lived communally in a large house in which Georgia city, now a museum?
questions.fact: Known as the Big House, it was a gathering place for the band, its families and friends in the early 1970s.

questions.prompt: Lynyrd Skynyrd's lineup in the 1970s was famous for how many guitarists?
questions.fact: Gary Rossington, Allen Collins and Ed King, and later Steve Gaines in King's place, gave the band its layered guitar sound.

questions.prompt: The 1983 ZZ Top album Eliminator is built around what kind of car?
questions.fact: The custom coupe starred on the cover and in the band's videos, and it was built for Billy Gibbons.

questions.prompt: Dickey Betts wrote the Allman Brothers instrumental "Jessica" for whom?
questions.fact: The sunny melody is often described as capturing the energy of a small child at play.

questions.prompt: The title of Lynyrd Skynyrd's 1973 debut album is what?
choices: A pronunciation guide to the band's name
A tribute to their high school coach

questions.fact: The title spelled out how to say the band's name, which fans and DJs often got wrong.

questions.prompt: Which Nashville event did Charlie Daniels host each year, bringing all-star friends on stage?
questions.fact: Started in the 1970s, the Volunteer Jam brought rock, country and bluegrass players into one long show.

questions.prompt: Molly Hatchet's album covers were painted by which fantasy artist?

questions.fact: Fans and critics have long noted the resemblance to Hooker's boogie groove.

questions.fact: Gibbons has long called it his favorite instrument, and its thick tone anchors many ZZ Top records.

questions.fact: Dowd had also engineered sessions for Ray Charles and Aretha Franklin at Atlantic.

questions.fact: Leavell's piano is a key part of Brothers and Sisters, and his Stones role began in the 1980s.

questions.prompt: Molly Hatchet's name comes from a folk legend about what?
choices: A woman who killed men with a hatchet
questions.fact: The band, formed in Jacksonville, Florida, took the grisly legend as a badge.

questions.prompt: Dickey Betts wrote "Blue Sky" about whom?
questions.fact: Betts has said the song honored Sandy Bluesky Wabegijig, and its twin-guitar harmony became a fan favorite.

questions.fact: The story is that he scribbled the lyrics at a desperate hour, and the song grew into a Fillmore East showpiece.

stories.title: Fillmore East, March 1971
stories.dek: Six musicians, two drummers and the best live album of its day
stories.body:
By the beginning of 1971 the Allman Brothers Band was a small group with a big reputation. They came from Macon, Georgia, where their label Capricorn Records had set up shop, and they were known as one of the best live bands in America. Duane Allman and Dickey Betts played lead guitar, Gregg Allman sang and played the Hammond B-3 organ, Berry Oakley played bass, and two drummers, Butch Trucks and Jaimoe, laid down the rhythm. Their first two studio albums had not sold well. On stage, though, they were something else.

The band's manager, Phil Walden, and producer Tom Dowd decided to capture them on tape at the Fillmore East, the New York theater run by promoter Bill Graham. The band played two nights, on March 12 and 13, 1971. The late shows ran into the early hours, and Dowd's team recorded every note.

What happened on those nights was a long, loose, joyful conversation between musicians who trusted each other. Duane's slide guitar and Betts's melodic leads wound around one another like two voices in harmony. They opened with "Statesboro Blues", a song by the old Georgia bluesman Blind Willie McTell. They played "Whipping Post", Gregg's song, which stretched past 22 minutes, and the instrumental "In Memory of Elizabeth Reed", which let the guitar players flow into jazz.

The result was At Fillmore East, released in July 1971. It reached the US Top 20, and it made the band stars. Critics later compared it to the best live records ever made, and it proved that a rock group could improvise at length without losing the song. It also set the template for Southern rock: dual lead guitars, twin drummers, and a blues feel.

The band played the closing night at the Fillmore East that June, when Graham shut the venue down, and they seemed to be on the verge of a long career. Then, on October 29, 1971, Duane Allman, 24 years old, was killed in a motorcycle accident in Macon. Berry Oakley died in a similar crash just over a year later, a few blocks away.

The band carried on, and its next studio album, Brothers and Sisters, brought them "Ramblin' Man", their biggest hit. Yet fans still return to those March nights, when the original lineup was at its best, and tape was running.

stories.title: Answering Neil Young
stories.dek: How "Sweet Home Alabama" came to be
stories.body:
In 1970 Neil Young released a song called "Southern Man". It was a hard look at racism in the American South, with Young's guitar growling behind a slow, ominous beat. Two years later he followed it with "Alabama", which asked the state some pointed questions. Many Southern musicians heard those songs as an outsider's lecture. One of them was Ronnie Van Zant, the singer for a Jacksonville band called Lynyrd Skynyrd.

Van Zant was proud of his home and bristled at the idea that the South could be dismissed in a song. By 1974 Skynyrd had a record deal and a loyal following, and they were working on their second album, Second Helping, at Studio One in Doraville, Georgia. Guitarist Ed King had been playing a bright riff in the studio, and Van Zant, Gary Rossington and King worked it into a song. Van Zant wrote lyrics with a fiercely proud tone. The song name-checked Neil Young and told him a Southern man didn't need him around.

The song had its own flavor. There was a line about Birmingham and its governor, a sly joke about Watergate ("Now Watergate does not bother me, does your conscience bother you?"), and a tip of the hat to the Swampers, the Muscle Shoals session musicians who had played on so many hits. Backing singers chanted "boo, boo, boo" in the background, and the song was given a swampy, upbeat bounce. Al Kooper, who produced the band, helped them polish it.

"Sweet Home Alabama" reached the US Top 10 that fall and became the band's signature song. It was often taken as a flat-out rebuttal to Young, but the story was more friendly than that. Van Zant said in interviews that he admired Young's music, and the song was meant more as a spirited reply than a feud.

The song has since taken on a life of its own, played at ballparks and weddings and everywhere in between. Few songs started as an argument and ended up as a party. This one did, and its famous opening riff is still one of the first things a guitar student learns.

stories.title: Three Days After Street Survivors
stories.dek: The 1977 crash that stopped Lynyrd Skynyrd
stories.body:
In the fall of 1977 Lynyrd Skynyrd was riding high. The band had spent several years touring relentlessly, and its albums sold well. A new record, Street Survivors, came out on October 17, 1977, and it sold briskly from the start. The cover showed the band standing in a wall of flames, a striking image. Guitarist Steve Gaines, who had joined the previous year, gave the group a new energy, and Ronnie Van Zant was writing some of his best songs, including "That Smell", which warned of the dangers of drink and drugs.

On October 20, the band was flying from Greenville, South Carolina, to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in a chartered Convair 240 propeller plane. Somewhere over Mississippi, the aircraft ran short of fuel. The pilots tried to reach an airport, and the engines failed. The plane came down in a swampy forest near Gillsburg, Mississippi.

Six people died: Ronnie Van Zant; Steve Gaines and his sister Cassie, who sang backup; assistant road manager Dean Kilpatrick; and the two pilots. Many others on board, including Gary Rossington, Allen Collins and Billy Powell, were badly injured but survived. The survivors spent months in hospitals, and some of them were permanently marked by their injuries.

The record company pulled the original Street Survivors cover with the flames, out of respect for those who had died, and replaced it with a plain black background. The album went platinum, and fans bought it in huge numbers. The band, however, was done. Remaining members drifted into other groups, such as the Rossington-Collins Band, and Allen Collins was left paralyzed in a car crash in 1986.

In 1987 the surviving members reunited for a tribute tour, with Ronnie's younger brother Johnny Van Zant on vocals. What was meant as a one-time event turned into a long-running revival, and the band continued to tour for decades with Rossington as its anchor.

Van Zant was 29 years old when he died. In his short life he had co-written some of rock's best-known songs, including "Free Bird", with guitarist Allen Collins, and "Sweet Home Alabama", with Gary Rossington and Ed King. The band's early records still sound alive, and at their concerts the crowd sings along to "Free Bird" as a tribute to the man who wrote it.

stories.title: ZZ Top Meets the Machine
stories.dek: How a blues trio from Texas learned to love synthesizers and video.
stories.body:
By the early 1980s ZZ Top had been playing Texas boogie for more than a decade. Guitarist Billy Gibbons, bassist Dusty Hill and drummer Frank Beard had built a following with records like Tres Hombres, and the long beards that Gibbons and Hill wore had become part of the look. The band took a break after 1981, and when they came back they wanted something different.

The result was Eliminator, recorded in Memphis at Ardent Studios with engineer Terry Manning and released in 1983. Gibbons has said the idea was to take their blues roots and mix them with modern technology. The record used synthesizers and sequenced parts alongside the usual crunchy guitar, and the drums were tightened to a steady, machine-like pulse. Frank Beard was a very good drummer, and he adjusted to the new tools.

The album came at the right moment, because MTV was growing and looking for videos with a clear story. ZZ Top supplied one. In clips for songs like Gimme All Your Lovin', Sharp Dressed Man and Legs, a young person in need of luck ends up with the keys to a gleaming red hot rod, a custom 1933 Ford coupe, thanks to the three bearded musicians. The band members do not say much, and the car, the beards and the hats did the talking. The simple idea worked, and it made the group easy to recognize at a glance.

Sharp Dressed Man is a good example of the approach. It has a thick, springy groove, a slick guitar part and a chorus that is easy to sing. The words are about looking sharp and feeling confident, and the video turns that into a small story about two young workers whose luck changes.

It could have been a risky move for a blues-rock band to embrace synthesizers. Instead, it widened ZZ Top's audience and introduced the group to a new generation of fans who knew them mainly from television. Gibbons has said that the guitar remained the heart of the music, and the best proof is the solo on Sharp Dressed Man.

Fans of the earlier records still have Tush and La Grange. But Eliminator showed that the band could change its sound without losing its sense of humor.

stories.title: Hold On Loosely
stories.dek: A band from Ronnie Van Zant's family tree finds a new sound.
stories.body:
When Lynyrd Skynyrd's plane went down in 1977, the world of Southern rock lost its best-known voice. Ronnie Van Zant had a younger brother, Donnie, who was leading a band called 38 Special out of Jacksonville, Florida. Donnie Van Zant and guitarist Don Barnes had formed the group in the mid-1970s, and their first records had the twin-guitar sound that fans of the genre expected.

Over the next few years the band went in a different direction. It was a smart move. The audience for long jams was shrinking, and radio wanted tighter songs with a bright, clean sound. 38 Special kept the Southern attitude, but they trimmed the arrangements and put more weight on hooks and harmony. Bassist Larry Junstrom had been in the earliest lineup of Skynyrd, so the band had real roots in the scene they were gently leaving behind.

The turning point was Hold On Loosely, on the 1981 album Wild-Eyed Southern Boys. The song was written by Barnes, guitarist Jeff Carlisi and Jim Peterik, a songwriter from Chicago who had been in the group Ides of March and who would soon help write Eye of the Tiger for Survivor. The advice in the title is about relationships: do not grip too tightly, or the thing you love will slip away. It is delivered over a crisp, driving riff.

Peterik had a talent for choruses, and his work with 38 Special shows it. He helped write several of the band's later songs, including Caught Up in You. Meanwhile, the group's producer, Rodney Mills, who had earlier engineered for Skynyrd, helped give the records a clean, radio-friendly sound without losing their punch.

38 Special was criticized by some Southern rock purists for being too polished. But the band never hid where it came from, and it kept the sound of two drummers on stage. Hold On Loosely became a favorite at their shows, and it remains the song most associated with the band.

Its story is a reminder that the music did not end with the plane crash. It grew into something new, with the same family and the same state of mind.

stories.title: The Devil Went Down to Georgia
stories.dek: A fiddle contest, a golden prize and a six-man writing credit.
stories.body:
Charlie Daniels had been a Nashville session player and a bandleader for years when he wrote one of the best-known story songs in country rock. The Devil Went Down to Georgia appeared in 1979 on the album Million Mile Reflections. It tells of a young fiddler named Johnny who takes on the Devil in a contest, with a golden fiddle on the line against Johnny's soul.

It is often said that the idea was influenced by Stephen Vincent Benet's poem about a fiddling contest, which also features a duel between a young player and a rival. He took that setup and moved it to Georgia, with a Devil in the role of the challenger. He and the band built the song out of the music, with each section of the arrangement acting like a scene in a short play.

The credit on the song is a clue to how it was made. Six musicians in the Charlie Daniels Band share the songwriting credit, including guitarist Tom Crain, keyboardist Taz DiGregorio, bassist Charlie Hayward, and drummers James W. Marshall and Fred Edwards. Daniels has described the song as a group effort, with the band helping shape the music while he handled the words and the fiddle.

The Devil's parts are played in a tense, driving style, with the band pushing and the fiddle snarling. When Johnny answers, the music lifts into a bright, fast reel, and the fiddle solos fly. There is real skill in the way the song moves from menace to triumph.

The song won a Grammy Award in 1980 for Best Country Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group, and it appeared in the film Urban Cowboy. It became a signature number for the band for the rest of its career, and Daniels played it at the end of many shows, often with a long fiddle breakdown.

The Devil Went Down to Georgia also showed how far country rock could travel. It was a story song with a big arrangement and a fiddle at the center, and it worked on country radio, rock radio and the dance floor.

stories.title: One More from the Road
stories.dek: Skynyrd at the Fox Theatre, summer of 1976.
stories.body:
In July 1976 Lynyrd Skynyrd went into the Fox Theatre in Atlanta to record a live album. They were at the top of their form, and they were playing in a city that treated them as hometown heroes. The Fox is an ornate theater from 1929, built like a palace, and it was saved from demolition in the 1970s after a public campaign. It was a fitting place for a Georgia band to make a record.

The group had a new lineup. Guitarist Ed King had left the year before, and Steve Gaines had joined, which gave Skynyrd three guitarists again: Gaines, Gary Rossington and Allen Collins. Billy Powell played keyboards, Leon Wilkeson bass and Artimus Pyle drums. A trio of backing singers called the Honkettes included Gaines's sister Cassie. Ronnie Van Zant stood at the center of the stage, and his easy, wry voice introduced the songs.

The set included the band's biggest numbers. Sweet Home Alabama and Gimme Three Steps drew shouts from the crowd, and Tuesday's Gone showed the slow side of the band. The set ended with Free Bird, which was stretched to over fourteen minutes and had the audience on its feet. The guitar solo that closes the song, with the three guitarists trading off, became one of the most imitated pieces of Southern rock.

The record came out in September 1976 as a double album called One More from the Road. It was well received, and it helped confirm Skynyrd's reputation as a great live act. The sound is raw and close, and it gives the feeling of being in the room.

The story has a sad ending. In October 1977, a little more than a year after the Fox recordings, the band's plane crashed in Mississippi, and Ronnie Van Zant, Steve Gaines and Cassie Gaines were among those who died. The live album captures the group at a moment that now seems especially precious, with all of its energy and its confidence.

The Fox Theatre remains an Atlanta landmark, and Free Bird there is still the version many fans think of first.

stories.title: Summer Jam at Watkins Glen
stories.dek: The largest crowd of the 1970s, three bands and a jam the day before.
stories.body:
On July 28, 1973, a crowd gathered at the Watkins Glen Grand Prix Raceway in upstate New York for an all-day concert with three bands: the Grateful Dead, the Band and the Allman Brothers Band. The promoters had reportedly sold about 150,000 tickets, but estimates of the crowd ran as high as 600,000, and many people arrived days early and camped in the fields.

The Allman Brothers were at an important point in their career. Duane Allman had died in 1971, and bassist Berry Oakley died in 1972. The band had carried on with Dickey Betts as the leading guitarist, Lamar Williams on bass, and pianist Chuck Leavell, and they were about to release the album Brothers and Sisters. It contained Ramblin' Man, a song that Betts had written and sang, and it would become the band's best-known single. At Watkins Glen they were playing it before it reached the public.

The festival is also remembered for what happened the day before. On Friday, members of the Dead, the Band and the Allman Brothers did a sound check that turned into a long jam, with the huge crowd already in the field. Fans who were there have said it felt as if the show had started early. Rock historians often mention the sound check as one of the most memorable moments of the weekend.

On Saturday the bands each played long sets, and the Allman Brothers brought their own mix of blues, country and jazz-inflected jams. Betts and Gregg Allman led, and the two drummers, Butch Trucks and Jaimoe, kept the groove going.

The sheer size of the crowd strained the roads and the supplies, but many who were there remember a peaceful scene.

Watkins Glen became a milestone for the Allman Brothers and for Southern rock. It showed that a band from Georgia could draw as many people as the biggest names in the country, and it helped set up the success of Ramblin' Man.
